newsitem.title: MONACO: OLYMPICS-IOC TO RULE ON BOXING SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC TO RULE ON BOXING SCANDAL.

text.p: Olympic chiefs rule on the 1988 Seoul Games boxing scandal this week.

Accusations that American light-middleweight Roy Jones was cheated out of a gold medal by bribed judges are believed to have been discussed at a meeting of International Olympic Committee legal experts on Monday.
IOC director general Francois Carrard later confirmed that Olympic chiefs would make a decision on the scandal during a three-day meeting of the executive board which started here on Monday.
"A decision will be made here," Carrard said. "By tomorrow hopefully but certainly during this executive board."
Last year the IOC appointed a commission to investigate the alleged corruption involving a number of ringside judges in Seoul.

One report on the affair, including documents obtained from the archives of former East Germany's secret police which took a great interest in sport, alleges somes judges were bribed in favour of South Koreans and that some international boxing officials were aware of the cheating.
Jones, who went on to become a professional world champion, was beaten in the 1988 final by South Korean Park Si-hun after an extraordinary decision.
Most spectators and commentators present had Jones way ahead of his outclassed opponent but three judges from Morocco, Uruguay and Uganda gave the decision to Park.
Last March, the IOC said it needed to talk to one key figure in the affair before it could announce the result of its findings. But it expected its final report to be ready in May.
At a time when more and more athletes are taking their disputes with sporting authorities to the civil courts, Olympic chiefs know they must take a decision which is legally watertight.
Carrard refused to say whether the IOC's juridical commission had discussed the case at its meeting early on Monday but one Olympic source confirmed it had been on the agenda.
